speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Hey, this is Carlos, CEO at Product School and your host on The Product Podcast. My guest today is Elaina O'Mahoney, Chief Product Officer at Mural. Her argument: visual collaboration has gone missing in the AI era. We are all working alone in a chat box, and ideas got so cheap that the real bottleneck moved to where decisions actually get made. Here's what we cover: why shared context is the new bottleneck, not creativity. Kill the five-page strategy doc, ship the prototype. The black market for tokens inside big enterprises. Why your best forward deployed engineer might sit in legal. And ask what did you learn, not what did you ship. Let's get into it.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Welcome to The Product Podcast, Elaina.

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: I'm so excited to be here. Thanks, Carlos.

text: So you're the Chief Product Officer at Mural, a product I've used for a very long time. When it started, the whole pitch was basically, "Hey, this is a better version of PowerPoint." But now this whole industry of visual collaboration has evolved quite a bit. I'd love to get your take on it.

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: Absolutely. It was meant really to collaborate about ideas, to brainstorm. Our co-creators are from Argentina. What's really interesting is when you work for an organization, or when you're a team trying to come up with a multitude of ideas, you're trying to brainstorm, converge, diverge, and then ultimately decide on a path forward. speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: Yeah, what's interesting is visual collaboration is actually absent in the AI era. We are all in our tools, all by ourselves, with words or voice. I don't know if you dictate to yourself too often or speak to your LLM of choice often. I probably do that more than type these days, but it's very lonely and it's not visual. And when I go to collaborate with my coworkers, I'm now sharing words in a doc, rather than understanding through visual collaboration and designing something more easily digestible to get to decision-making faster.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Now you're bringing up the point on multiplayer, and we've been talking about this for a long time. At the beginning it was more of an idea. I see a lot of people still using visual collaboration tools, PowerPoints, or Google Docs in the same way as putting comments on the side. speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: It's really interesting, because now ideas are really cheap. You can go from an idea to an actual working prototype in hours, or write a doc, or create a slide deck in minutes. So for us, and when we're thinking about our product process, we almost have to forget the process part. We have to create a system that really enables faster decision-making now that ideas are cheap. How do you take all of these different artifacts spatially and connect them together so people have the same context? Because that's what the game is about now: am I playing the same game as you are, and do I actually know where you started? Can I catch up to you as fast as you are, so we can just make decisions faster, because you have so many more decisions to make? Shared Context Is the New Bottleneck

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Yes. And I see that the same way as in the past, a lot of these SaaS companies were trying to replace the spreadsheet. speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: The competitive landscape is really interesting, because when you're a product leader, a lot of your skill set is about future casting. You have to create these strategies that are two to five years forward, but it's almost an in-the-moment feedback loop that you now need to create with system-level thinking. So for us, it's really just about having the right information in the right moment in time. For example, if I start with a document and then I want to spatially present that idea to multiple people, can I quickly turn that document into a prototype, into slides? And can I connect them spatially together so everybody has the same context to make the right decision moving forward?

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I see companies like Slack or Teams trying to be that space for people to collaborate. You also have issue-tracking tools like Jira or Linear trying to communicate, "This is the place where work gets done." But the reality is it's still unclear where work gets done, where agents are being deployed, as companies try to truly deploy this in a way that drives adoption. It's not just a few people creating their own context. Where does work happen, and how does the right flow of information have to go?

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: Yeah, it's an interesting concept, where every tool right now in the stack is almost converging in a circular area, and everybody is also converging on a chat-widget UI where work happens. How many different companies have the same tagline of "where work happens"? OKRs can be in a certain area, and it'll say what work is planned, and then you can measure against what's been planned. Slack is very good for communication in the moment. Then you'll have Notion, Confluence, Docs, Jira, or Linear, where you're still planning work or capturing decisions that have been made. The space that really is still ambiguous is how decisions are getting made and the context of why. That's a blank canvas area we think we're converging on. Yes, in meetings we talk about stuff, but the meeting notes come after; they capture a summary. You still don't have the context of why the decision was made. So how do you bring some of this disparate information together and really get to the why behind decision-making in the moment? When AI Is a Layer, Not a Button

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: You're making me think about how some of these products that try to become the center of where work happens started implementing AI. It was usually a button that said "AI," with a star; you click it and it summarizes information or does something magical. But now it feels like AI is not just a button. It happens across the board, and maybe some of the things don't need to be called AI at all. So as you think about the user who hasn't set up the context, the one who shows up and is suddenly in a canvas where they can start playing around with different pieces of information: for product teams specifically, how do you see that happening today when they're maybe not super technical, maybe not a designer, but they still need to ship stuff and not depend on the next person in line to slow them down?

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: Yeah, we have this arm of our business we call LUMA. It's one of our services offerings now that we're part of this organization, really going through LUMA practitioner training. Something we try to break away from is people thinking they're not a designer. If you've put together a slide deck, if you've done a drawing, and everybody drew when they were a kid, you're a designer at heart. So everybody actually needs to embrace the fact that they are a designer. You may not do it by trade, and you may not do it to the proficiency of those in the design community, but everybody can design, and there are tools out there that can help you. The point is that visual pictures, whether it's a customer journey map, a diagram, or even a data analytics diagram, let you absorb information faster than if you were to read a document. It's that visual element of being able to contextualize information much quicker that really speeds up your ideation process, speeds up how you make decisions, what you decide to take to market. Now that I work at Mural and I do that more frequently than I did previously, I can see how we can get to the disagreements faster. How do we get to where the challenges and bottlenecks are so much faster when it's visual? Leading by Example: Everybody Should Be Shipping

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: What you just said about leading by example sets the tone. I've hosted product leaders from Tropic, Vercel, and other AI-native companies, and they're all shipping from top to bottom, right to left. Everybody is a builder in a way. So I'm curious to know, for you personally as the Chief Product Officer, how do you actually set that tone?

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: Yeah, absolutely. I do think everybody should be playing and shipping now. Should everybody be shipping in production all the time? Maybe. The lens is where you can ship in safe environments. You can actually solve some of your core bottlenecks as the CPO, where you inherently would make decisions and choices. You can democratize some of that by just shipping workflows, shipping agents, shipping research agents. There are still some things that are quite scarce that you can work on internally. Data science is still scarce. Really good taste is still scarce. Synthesizing analytics is still scarce. So you can actually decide as a CPO where you play in that space to make your team's techniques faster.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I just had this recent example today. I shipped the new email signature for the company. I didn't really ship it into production; it was like 80%. But I felt unstoppable, because I could express myself in a much more visual way. So now we're going to skip a couple of steps. Ultimately there's an expert who's still going to validate it, and another expert who's going to put it into production. But first of all, it feels great.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: It's not a major, major release. But I like your point that shipping doesn't need to be something major into production. Shipping a workflow is still a great way to demo that you can do it. Kill the Five-Page Strategy Doc, Ship the Prototype

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: Yeah, it's also something we went through here at Mural, which hopefully is relevant to other product leaders and to engineering, design, and product teams. Usually a product leader would write this very, very big product strategy doc. Sometimes it's five pages, sometimes it's four pages. It makes the rounds, people comment, and maybe it starts to slowly die. What we can actually do faster as leaders is create a prototype of something we're envisioning. I'm not saying it will ship like this prototype, but it conveys some of the principles that you want the teams to explore, and a North Star direction. You as the product leader can do that so much faster. Or you as the PM, or even the engineer, could say, "Hey, what about this concept and idea?" And it actually moves the entire team faster in their ideation cycle, or their decision-making cycle, just with a visual.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

Creating a Safe Space to Try and Fail Elaina O'Mahoney | Mural 00:14:42 Yeah, I think it's actually lowering the bar for somebody to learn in a lower-risk environment. What AI has created is almost the haves, where you have to virtue signal that you're always ahead of the game, on the frontier, versus those who are like, "I think I can write my emails and do the summaries, and I can even write a Slack bot that summarizes the things I need to do in the morning." text: A lot of the companies we guide are large enterprises, and we try to bring the right tools for them. speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney

That's the hardest struggle for very large enterprise organizations: they're keeping their process, but then trying to adapt to a new way of learning while keeping that process. text: And for that type of system, do you require some type of forward deployed engineers at some point, or is it something you think can be done a little more organically?

text: I think forward deployed engineers are really, really helpful, because they're usually the ones who can use the tools that are best for the job today. I now can do a bit of what they did." So whether it's a forward deployed engineer, or somebody in legal that's automated their process, it doesn't necessarily have to be an engineer. text: Yeah, I think it's about being able to create a forum for people to showcase their work. And I hate to keep saying Mural, but it's a collaborative tool; you can see what people are doing. He is so good here. He's automated 50% of our processes already." And when I think back, it's actually probably better that he's there automating a different part of our business than me stealing him for us. But he's able to showcase his work in Mural. He shares it with the entire organization, and it gives people these lightbulb moments in every department. Tapping the Community Without Chasing ROI

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: One of the things I think is unique about your product is the community aspect. So I'm curious to know how you're tapping into that open community of people using Mural, to then bring some of those best practices to the way you build the product, or the way other companies should be using it.

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: Yeah, we've actually introduced a newer community within Mural, and we've got a subset of our customers who are first invited to it. That ties back to the previous point I was making: it's about sharing how you're working, how you're deciding, how you're thinking. It's the same reason you exist, Carlos. You've created this community where people can share ideas about how they work, and it sparks another idea in another company, from another person. The thing I was most surprised about when I joined Mural a little more than a year and a half ago is how many people are so passionate about human-centered design, visual collaboration, ensuring people can all feel like designers, and that ideas can come from everywhere.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I ask you that question because it's an important piece of how I think about my business. When I started thinking about building community for our company, I didn't have any expectation in return. I knew I had to find a way to measure ROI, and at some point I couldn't. I was like, "You know what? I don't know how to measure it, but we're still going to do it." And I think that sparked something. Sure, it'd be great to say it reduces customer support or increases revenue, and I'm sure there are some derivatives to that. But actually giving value is critical, because there are so many other options out there. Why would someone dedicate time to build and share what they're doing with your product?

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: Yeah, it can serve multiple purposes. A community that inspired me earlier on was Lenny's community. It's creating this trusting, open environment where people can say, "I've tested this out, I've done it this way," or you can ask a more vulnerable question, and people are there to almost say, "I know an answer, I've tried it this way," or "I can connect you with somebody else. Do you want me to show you?" It's the value of that loop that's actually quicker, because you're getting it from people not inside your echo chamber. The Black Market for Tokens

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I want to connect this to how you're thinking about pricing. At some point, if you can really drive adoption within your business and you build the right integrations, you're unstoppable; people need that product to survive. It's the heart of how they build. So how are you thinking about pricing now, with token usage and everything?

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: This is the thing that actually keeps me up at night. I wonder how many organizations that are, to use the very vibe name, "AI-native." We weren't born when tokens and LLMs were there. So our pricing model reflects a lot of the seat-based pricing that everybody now attaches to legacy SaaS. But there's almost a double-edged sword with usage. When we speak to some of our larger customers, there's almost a black market for tokens. If they use their own tokens, they'll have to go to three other employees to say, "I've got 80% of the way there with my prototype, and my tokens got cut off. Susie, can I siphon some of your tokens?" And now it disincentivizes the wrong behavior. So it's a decision we're taking with the utmost care. It goes back to the fact that we serve totally different types of businesses, from a person who just bought us for themselves, for their three-person company or even their solo consulting gig, all the way up to a Fortune 500 company with 10,000 people. We have to think of pricing models throughout that same range, and maybe the pricing models are completely different. We know the value of our product in this very near future has to be filled with AI at its core, but we also don't want to disincentivize folks from using it and have to keep an accounting ledger of tokens. Making Sure Usage Drives the Right Outcomes

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: We're at the early innings of this. You see the examples of companies that are burning tokens and are very proud of it. But I also know companies that send the right mandate, like "You have to burn X amount of tokens." I'm not going to mention those companies, but they game their own system, kind of like in the past when some salespeople would report fake calls on their CRM to show product activity. Now they're trading whatever it is on AI to say, "Hey, I burnt X amount of tokens." So how do you ensure that some of this usage is actually driving the right business outcomes?

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: I think the first thing comes with measurement, which was actually the first inclination of most organizations: "Here's a tool, just use it." And usage showed adoption, and then everybody's like, "Holy crap, this is very expensive. Pull back, pull back, pull back." So it's really about starting with a measurement layer, and then measuring how they're using it. Just because you can with AI, and I'm probably going to say the controversial thing, doesn't mean you need to do it with AI. Maybe spell check with AI is quite expensive. There are other things that can do spell check that don't have AI. So can we apply it to the right things? Can we at least measure our costs? Everything is going to come back to learning loops at the moment, that give us the flexibility of decision-making and don't go too far down the future casting of decision-making, because it's really hard to pull back pricing models. Once pricing models are in the air, people are really going to fight tooth and nail to not change them. And the last thing we're trying to make sure of is predictability. Any business has to understand its cost when things are so uncertain. So the cost of our tool can't wildly swing from month to month at all. There has to be predictability to it, so they can continue investing, so it can incentivize the right usage behavior, and people can get value out of it freely. How Mural Structures Its Product Teams

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Can you give me a sense for the current team that you run?

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: The current team that I run really focuses on both broad capabilities and very specific personas, because we're a very broad-based tool. We have some traditional triad teams, with designers, engineers, and product folks. Then we have some product engineers playing dual roles, and some designer-product folks playing hybrid roles. It completely depends on the area of the business you work in. If you're within our core product that serves all of our users, we're going to have more of a traditional triad, because you can't just frontier-test and try with, say, banking and finance organizations that have to go through a lot of administrative and security processes. But if we're in a newer area of the business where we're trying things out, we can go to hugely untraditional models, where you have different hybrid teams that can ship to production very, very fast, and change management isn't really part of that issue. It's high experimentation. So we run that gamut of teams working completely differently depending on the outcome they're trying to drive.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Ultimately, you oversee the different teams, right? Zero-to-one, and the more core product.

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: Absolutely. I take it from the model of a city planner. You have a working city, so the way you change it has to be more thought through. If you're going to break down a freeway and put in a new one, or make a toll bridge, that's different from being a frontier team. The frontier team is back in the day before America was America, heading out West. You have to backpack, you have to kill your own food, you have to forage. The way those two teams work is completely, oppositely different, but they're serving the same business. Balancing Core Business Against Future Bets

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I was having a similar conversation with the CEO at ServiceNow, a public company over $100 billion in market cap, but down at least 25% year to date. When you have that type of market pressure, I was trying to understand how much effort you put on the future, knowing it might not pay off next quarter. In your case, as a private company, I'm curious how you allocate those resources: new bets, or things that are less mature, versus things that keep the lights on.

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: Yeah, it's the innovator's dilemma. You have a business you need to serve today that's reinforcing your revenue stream, but you know you want to evolve your product and service for a possibly totally different audience. So you have to really think of the allocation in bets. Maybe we do a certain percentage for bets that we know could be self-fulfilling, without forgetting our core business and why people buy us today. So it's really about spreading that allocation of bets, and letting the team within that bet area help us understand what's working and what's not, and whether we need to reallocate those dollars. That decision-making is much, much faster. I'm paying attention to a lot of that future bet of what's working. How do we make something that's maybe completely different than what we do today, but stays core to collaboration, bringing people together, and visual? It's really that bet allocation. But you have to look at revenue. Ask "What Did You Learn?" Not "What Did You Ship?"

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Exactly. So traditionally there would be these big QBRs, maybe annual planning. I'd love to know how often you reprioritize now.

speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
text: Oh, that's probably once a month. On the future-bet casting, that feedback loop is once a month. Our CTO and myself are meeting with the teams to say, "What did we learn?" We're not just saying "What did you ship?" It's "What did you learn?" Because you need to change your decision-making faster. If we're not changing our decision-making, or we're still thinking the same way we did a month ago, we didn't gather the right information. It has to be something net new. So meeting with our future-bet teams once a month helps reinforce that feedback loop, and helps us decide, "Oh, maybe we need more resources in this future bet, because they're onto something." It's almost like running three mini-startups inside a business that's been around for over ten years.
